readerTitle: The opera house that opened ten years late
caseNote: 실제 사례 (시드니 오페라하우스 건설) + 실제 연구 (Buehler 외 1994) + 가상 적용 (마케팅 에이전시, 레스토랑 2호점)
insight: 일정과 예산은 내 계획의 단계를 더해서가 아니라, 비슷한 일이 실제로 얼마나 걸렸는지에서 출발해 잡는다.
misconception: 계획을 더 자세히 세우면 일정이 정확해진다. 이번 프로젝트는 지난번과 다르니 지난 지연은 참고할 필요가 없다.

sources.text: Kahneman, D. & Tversky, A. (1979). Intuitive prediction: Biases and corrective procedures. TIMS Studies in Management Science, 12, 313–327.
Buehler, R., Griffin, D. & Ross, M. (1994). Exploring the "planning fallacy": Why people underestimate their task completion times. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 67(3), 366–381.
Sydney Opera House, official history (design competition 1957, construction 1959, opening 1973)
Flyvbjerg, B. (2006). From Nobel Prize to project management: Getting risks right. Project Management Journal, 37(3). (reference class forecasting, outside view)

factChecks.note: 시드니 오페라하우스: 1957년 설계 공모 선정, 당초 목표 1963년 완공·약 A$7백만, 실제 1973년 10월 개관·약 A$1억 2백만. 자료마다 초기 예산 표기(£3.5백만 ≈ A$7백만)가 다르므로 공식 역사 자료로 다시 확인하세요. 102 ÷ 7 ≈ 14.6배.
착공 1959년(설계 미완성 상태), Jørn Utzon 사임 1966년. 공식 역사 자료로 확인 필요.
Buehler 외(1994) 졸업논문 연구: 평균 예상 약 33.9일, 실제 약 55.5일, 예상 기한 내 완료 약 30%, '최악의 경우' 예상 평균 약 48.6일. 원문 수치를 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 반올림해 34일, 56일, 49일로 적었습니다.
'planning fallacy'라는 용어는 Kahneman & Tversky(1979)에서 처음 쓰였다는 것이 통설입니다. 원문 확인 필요.
에이전시 선택지 B의 버퍼 계산: 6주 → 7주는 약 17% 증가(카드에는 'small cushion'으로만 표기). 지난 프로젝트 9·10·12주는 계획 대비 50~100% 초과. 모두 가상 수치.

cards.title: The opera house that opened ten years late
body: In 1957, Sydney chose a bold design for a new opera house. The plan was to finish by 1963 for about A$7 million.
It opened in 1973. The final bill was about A$102 million. The people behind it weren't careless. They made a mistake almost everyone makes.

image.label: Harbour opera house half-built, with a calendar flipping from 1963 to 1973
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 조개껍데기 모양 지붕의 오페라하우스가 비계에 둘러싸여 반쯤 지어진 모습. 옆에 큰 달력이 1963에서 1973으로 넘어가는 모션. 실제 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: How long should you promise?
body: You run a small marketing agency. A client wants a new brand identity and website. Your team lists every task and adds them up: 6 weeks.
Your last three similar projects took 9, 10 and 12 weeks. Each had its own surprise. What deadline do you give the client?

options.text: 6 weeks. This plan is more detailed than the last ones
options.feedback: A detailed plan feels safe, but the last three felt detailed too. You'd win trust today and likely spend it around week seven.

options.text: 7 weeks: the plan plus a small buffer
options.feedback: Better than no buffer. But a one-week cushion is small next to your own history of running 50% or more over.

options.text: About 10 weeks, based on how long similar projects actually took
options.feedback: You may sound slower than a rival. But you're planning from what happens, not from what you hope will happen.

cards.title: Sydney's surprises weren't really surprising.
body: Construction started in 1959, before the design was finished. Nobody yet knew how to build the famous roof shells. Solving that alone took years.
Costs rose, politics got tense, and the architect, Jørn Utzon, resigned in 1966. Each problem felt like bad luck. But a huge, first-of-its-kind building running into problems was close to certain.

cards.title: The planning fallacy
body: The **planning fallacy** is our habit of underestimating how long a task will take and what it will cost, even when we know similar tasks ran late. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky named it in 1979.
The cause is the *inside view*. We picture our own steps going roughly to plan. Delays, sick days and rework don't feel like part of the plan, so they never make it in.

image.label: Inside view: a straight path. Outside view: winding paths of past projects
image.brief: 좌우 분할 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Inside view": 출발점에서 목표까지 곧게 뻗은 한 줄. 오른쪽 "Outside view": 비슷한 과거 프로젝트 여러 개의 구불구불하고 더 긴 경로가 겹쳐 보임. 오른쪽 경로들의 끝이 왼쪽보다 훨씬 멀리 있음.

cards.title: Even the worst case was too hopeful.
body: In a 1994 study, Roger Buehler and colleagues asked students when they would finish their final-year thesis. The average guess was about 34 days. The average actual time was about 56.

Only about 30% finished by their own estimate. Even their *if everything goes badly* guesses, about 49 days, were too short. The students knew past projects had run late. They just believed this one would be different.

cards.title: Start from the outside view.
body: Before looking at your own plan, ask how long similar projects usually take. Researchers call this the **outside view**.
list: **Find comparisons:** past jobs like this one, yours or other people's
**Start from their real results:** time, cost, how often they ran over
**Then adjust:** only for specific, real differences in this project
cards.callout: Your plan tells you the best path. Past projects tell you the usual one.
cards.softwareNote: Software teams meet this constantly. Checking how long past features of similar size actually took gives a better starting point than adding up task estimates.

cards.title: The outside view has its own traps.
body: It only works if the comparisons are fair. Ten past jobs that were much smaller than this one will still mislead you.

Honest estimates also cost something. A longer quote can lose a bid to a rival who promises less. Often the better move is to quote a range or cut scope, not to pad silently. And a buffer nobody manages tends to get used up early.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant.
body: You're opening a second location. The contractor says the fit-out will take 8 weeks.
You need to set an opening date, hire staff and book a launch night. What's your plan?

options.text: Open at week 8. The contractor does this for a living
options.feedback: Contractors plan from the inside view too. If it runs late, you pay new staff to wait and cancel a launch you've already promoted.

options.text: Ask the contractor and other owners how long recent fit-outs really took, and set the date from that
options.feedback: It takes a few calls and may push your date back. In return, staff, rent and marketing line up with a date you can actually hit.

options.text: Open at week 9 to leave one week spare
options.feedback: A buffer helps, but one week is a guess. Without real past fit-outs to compare, you can't tell if it's enough.

cards.title: Plan from what usually happens, not what should happen.
body: Start with how long similar projects really took. Then adjust for what's truly different this time.
**Try it today:** pick one deadline you've set. Find two or three past projects like it and check how long they actually took.
